title: Seven Indian Americans Named to Cancer Care's Most Coveted Under-40 List
excerpt: The AVBCC's 2026 honours spotlight a generation of diaspora physicians reshaping American oncology—from financial toxicity to TikTok outreach
body:
When the Association for Value-Based Cancer Care (AVBCC) released its 2026 "40 Under 40 in Cancer" list—culled from roughly 2,800 nominations—seven of the names it printed were of Indian origin. The awardees will be honoured on May 30 at the Palmer House in Chicago, but the significance of their selection reverberates well beyond a single ballroom. It is the latest, and perhaps most concentrated, proof that Indian-American physicians now occupy a structural role at the frontier of American oncology.

The seven span the discipline's full arc. Dr Vishnukamal Golla, a clinical urologist who also works in health policy at Evolent, studies financial toxicity—the debt spiral that cancer diagnosis can set off in American households. Dr Puneeth Indurlal, vice-president of practice operations at the American Oncology Network, designs the alternative payment models that could eventually defuse it. Where Golla and Indurlal attack the economics of treatment, Dr Urvi Shah at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center pursues its biology from an unconventional angle, investigating metabolic health and dietary interventions for multiple myeloma.

Then there is Dr Sanjay Juneja, a triple board-certified hematologist-oncologist at Mary Bird Perkins Cancer Center in Louisiana, whose digital platform TheOncDoc has reached more than half a million people worldwide. In an age when medical misinformation travels faster than peer-reviewed research, Juneja's video explainers have turned him into a rare thing: a credible oncologist with a mass audience. Dr Milan Thakor, founder of Colla Mental Health, tackles the psychological dimension of cancer, building mental-health support programmes tailored to patients undergoing treatment—a niche that mainstream oncology has been slow to formalise.

Dr Paul Singh, US medical director for multiple myeloma at AstraZeneca, works the clinical-trial end, shaping the strategy that determines which experimental therapies reach patients. And Dr Sundeep Grandhe, quadruple board-certified and trained at Sri Ramachandra Medical College in Chennai before completing his American residency, practises culturally responsive palliative medicine—care that accounts for the patient's language, faith and family structure, not merely their tumour.

## A Pipeline With Deep Roots

The numbers behind this recognition are not accidental. Indian-origin physicians make up roughly five per cent of America's medical workforce, a share more than three times their proportion of the general population. In certain sub-specialties—cardiology, anaesthesiology and, increasingly, oncology—the over-representation is starker still. The pipeline begins with India's ruthlessly competitive medical entrance exams, continues through gruelling residencies in American teaching hospitals, and feeds a culture in which medicine remains the diaspora's most prestigious career path.

What is newer is the breadth of influence. A generation ago, Indian-American doctors were celebrated primarily as skilled clinicians. The AVBCC list suggests their ambitions have broadened. Financial toxicity research, value-based payment models, digital health outreach, mental-health integration—these are system-level concerns, not bedside ones. The honourees are not simply treating cancer; they are redesigning the infrastructure around it.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly five million Indian Americans in the United States, the practical upside is tangible. Culturally competent physicians—those who understand vegetarian dietary constraints during chemo, or the role of extended family in care decisions—remain in short supply. Doctors like Grandhe, whose palliative practice explicitly incorporates cultural context, fill a gap that mainstream oncology rarely acknowledges.

There is a symbolic dimension, too. Cancer touches every community, and seeing Indian-origin names on a prestigious national list signals belonging in a way that quieter professional milestones do not. For younger NRIs weighing career choices, the AVBCC recognition offers a counter-narrative to the tech-startup glamour that has dominated recent diaspora success stories.

The ceremony at the Palmer House on May 30 will be brief, the applause polite. The real impact is structural: a generation of Indian-American physicians is embedding itself not at the margins of American cancer care but at its decision-making core—shaping how it is paid for, talked about, researched and, ultimately, delivered.
